turns.name: P1-intro
turns.question: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: pick the project that best shows my mobile skills
card.say: The AI trip planner at KKday is the one I'd pick. Travelers used it in our Android app to plan a trip they could actually book. They typed something like "Tokyo, 5,000 yuan, three days", and the app built a plan from real products. My responsibility started at the technical design and ended at launch. I designed the agent, built the core backend, and wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer's follow-up on this project.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names a real Android project (KKday AI trip planner), identifies users (travelers), the problem (planning a bookable trip from a budget/prompt), and the candidate's scope (technical design through launch, agent design, backend, Android streaming code), with no invented employers, titles, or numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY introduces one real Android project from the candidate's background with its users, the problem and the candidate's own scope; no invented employers, titles or numbers.

turns.name: P1-dyn
turns.question: On the AI trip planner at KKday, you said you designed the agent, built the core backend, and wrote the Android code reading the streamed plan — which of those did you personally build versus the team?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: which parts did you personally build
card.say: I personally built three parts. First, the agent design: how it reads the request, picks real products and checks the plan. Second, the core backend, including the personalization data layer. Third, the Android code that reads the SSE stream and shows the day cards. The app team built the other screens, and the merchant side was not mine.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer's follow-up on this project.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer directly addresses which parts were personally built, adds specifics (SSE stream, day cards, personalization data layer, app team's other screens, merchant side excluded) beyond the earlier answer, stays consistent with the prior claim of designing the agent, building the core backend, and writing the Android streaming code, and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-change
turns.question: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: pick a change you personally made, walk one user action through
card.say: The change I made myself is the SKU calculation on the product page. A user taps a date, a package or a ticket type, and the price and stock update. Before, every tap recalculated all combinations on the main thread and parsed the same JSON again. I flattened the configuration, built a price and stock index once, moved the work to Dispatchers.Default, and sent results out through StateFlow. Tap to finished screen went from about one second to 300 milliseconds.
card.then: Next I can explain how the index is built, or how the UI stays correct when the user taps fast.

more: The index is built once, and a tap just looks up the result. The heavy work runs on Dispatchers.Default, and the UI only collects from StateFlow.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer traces a tap through UI, state (StateFlow), and data/threading layers, names the specific logic changed (SKU calculation, index building, moving work off the main thread), and gives concrete before/after behavior. It does not invent numbers beyond the stated latency improvement, and it stays focused on the candidate's own change.
judge.criterion: SAY traces one user action through concrete layers (UI, state, data or network) and says which logic the candidate changed; separates own work from the team's; no invented numbers.

turns.name: P2-bug
turns.question: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: hardest bug to reproduce, what I suspected, what proved me wrong
card.say: The hardest one was a plan that looked fine but had a product that couldn't be booked. I first suspected the AI model, because the text read well. Then I replayed the saved request and response, and the model was fine. The real cause was our check: it compared product IDs as text, so "0123" and "123" passed as different products. I fixed the check to compare IDs as numbers, and added a test with that case.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a clear timeline — first suspicion (the AI model), the evidence that overturned it (replaying the saved request and response showed the model was fine), and the root cause (ID comparison as text, "0123" vs "123"). It distinguishes observation (the model was fine, IDs passed as different) from conclusion (the real cause was the check), and says nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY gives a timeline: first suspicion, the evidence (log, experiment or repro) that overturned it, and the root cause, distinguishing observation from conclusion.

turns.name: P2-dyn
turns.question: You said replaying the saved request and response proved the model was fine — how did you confirm the "0123" vs "123" mismatch was actually the cause, rather than just a plausible theory?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: how did you confirm the ID mismatch was the cause
card.say: I took the same saved request and ran it through the check twice. First with the IDs as text, and it passed. Then I changed only the comparison to numbers, and it failed with the right error. That was the only change, so the comparison was the cause. I also added a test with "0123" and "123" so it can't come back.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer builds directly on the candidate's earlier replay finding, adds a specific controlled experiment (running the same saved request with only the comparison changed from text to numbers), stays consistent with the KKday trip planner and the "0123"/"123" bug, and is technically sound without inventing any employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-alt
turns.question: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: other options, why not them, how did you know it worked after release
card.say: There were two other options. One was to keep the old calculation and just cache the result, but the first tap would still be slow. The other was to move the calculation to the backend, but that adds a network round trip on every tap. So I kept it on the phone with a prebuilt index. After release, I went through the booking flow myself and switching options felt smooth.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names two real alternatives (cache the old calculation; move calculation to the backend) with the constraints that ruled them out (first tap still slow; network round trip per tap), and gives a source of post-release result (personal walkthrough of the booking flow) — though it lacks a metric and its limits, it covers at least two of the listed elements correctly and says nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY names a real alternative and the constraint that ruled it out, and the source of the result (metric, test, ticket or feedback) with its limits.

turns.name: P3-risk
turns.question: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: delivery risk, team disagreed, who decided
card.say: At Debon Securities, I was moving the trading app to new navigation. During testing I found some old pages had a broken back button. I told the project manager that same day, before I had checked every page. I gave two options: keep the old pages and ship the rest this week, or delay the whole release. He chose to keep the old pages.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a concrete Debon Securities case, states he told the project manager the same day, offers two options, notes the PM decided, and describes his own action of flagging it before checking every page.
judge.criterion: SAY describes one concrete case: when and whom the candidate told, the options offered, who had the decision, and what the candidate personally did; attributes the case to the right company.

turns.name: P3-dyn
turns.question: You said the PM chose to keep the old pages and ship the rest — what risk were you willing to accept there, and who watched the data after release? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: what risk I accepted, who watched the data, what signal would pause or roll back
card.say: The risk I accepted was that some old pages still had the broken back button. I told the PM that clearly, and he decided to ship the rest. I kept checking the remaining pages and fixed the back button myself. My change went out in the next release, after it was tested. For the release, we ran the main flows before shipping: open a stock, go back, and check the watchlist.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: FAIL: The answer repeats the earlier risk and PM decision, and it never says who watched the data after release or what signal would have triggered a pause or rollback; it also adds a vague "next release" detail without addressing the question.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W1-scope
turns.question: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend system and failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.heard: switch to design exercise, clarify requirements, define MVP path
card.say: Okay, let's design the wallet. First, the scope I'd confirm. The MVP is one user path: send money to another person. The user picks a contact, enters an amount, confirms on a native screen, and sees the result. Does that match what you want?
card.then: Wait for the interviewer to confirm or add requirements.

judge.detail:
PASS: The answer proposes one MVP path (send money to a contact) and asks a scope-confirming question, though it covers only one of the listed clarification examples—still meets the "at least two if listed" bar? No—wait, the criterion lists four examples and requires at least two. The answer only touches scope confirmation generally without covering two specific listed items (balance vs rail, currency, offline, ledger authority). Re-evaluating: it proposes the MVP path correctly and asks a clarifying question, but covers fewer than two listed clarification examples. FAIL.

FAIL: Proposes the
judge.criterion: SAY asks clarifying questions about scope (stored balance vs external rail, currency, offline behaviour, authority of the ledger) and proposes one MVP path such as send money to a contact.

turns.name: W2-design
turns.question: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend system and failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a known contact, with a result screen that shows success, failure, processing or unknown", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: requirements given, draw client, server, local storage
card.say: Okay, I'll draw the three parts and what each one owns. The app owns the screens and a local database. The local database is only a cache of what the server told us.
card.type: draw@wallet architecture: flowchart TD ⏎   A[App screens: send, result, history] --> B[ViewModel] ⏎   B --> C[Repository] ⏎   C --> D[(Local DB: cached balance and history)] ⏎   C --> E[Wallet API client] ⏎   E --> F[Wallet server: ledger and limits] ⏎   F --> G[(Ledger DB)]
card.then: Next I'd cover the data model and how the server keeps a balance from going negative.

more: The server owns the real ledger and the limits. The app only shows what the server told it. The local database is just a cache, so the UI reads from one place.

diagram.type: draw@wallet architecture: flowchart TD ⏎   A[App screens: send, result, history]

judge.detail: PASS: The TYPE is a mermaid flowchart covering app screens, ViewModel, repository, local DB, API client, server, and ledger DB; SAY states the app owns screens and a local cache, and that the server owns the authoritative ledger and limits.
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of the Android client (UI, ViewModel, repository, local database), the server and its ledger; SAY says what each part owns and that the server ledger is the authority.

turns.name: W2-seq
turns.question: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend system and failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a known contact, with a result screen that shows success, failure, processing or unknown", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars
card.say: I'll draw the sequence for A sending B 80 dollars. A confirms on the native screen, and the app sends the request with a client transfer ID. The server checks A's balance, then debits A and credits B in one transaction. A ends at 20 dollars and B at 80 dollars. The server returns the transfer record, and the app saves it and shows the result screen.
card.type: draw@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as A's app ⏎   participant S as Wallet server ⏎   participant L as Ledger DB ⏎   A->>S: POST transfer, client ID, 8000 cents ⏎   S->>L: check A balance, debit A, credit B ⏎   L-->>S: committed ⏎   S-->>A: transfer record, status success ⏎   A->>A: save record, show result screen
card.then: Next: what the result screen shows if the response never comes back.

more: The sequence is on the board now. The next thing I'd cover is the failure path: what the app shows when the response is lost.

diagram.type: draw@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as A's app ⏎   particip

judge.detail: PASS: The TYPE mermaid sequenceDiagram covers confirm (A confirms on native screen), submit with client transfer ID (POST transfer, client ID, 8000 cents), atomic server debit and credit (check A balance, debit A, credit B in one transaction), the response (transfer record, status success), and the result (save record, show result screen); SAY covers amounts in cents (8000 cents) and final balances (A 20 dollars, B 80) and result states.
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid sequenceDiagram covering confirm, submit with a client transfer ID, an atomic server debit and credit, the response and the result; SAY covers amounts in cents and the final balances (A 20 dollars, B 80) and the result states.

turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the app sends the request with a client transfer ID — what exactly is stored locally before that request goes out, and how does the app use that ID when the response is lost?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend system and failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a known contact, with a result screen that shows success, failure, processing or unknown", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: what is stored locally before the request, and how the ID is used when the response is lost
card.say: Before the request goes out, I save a pending transfer row in the local database. It holds the client transfer ID, the recipient, the amount in cents, and a status of pending. The ID is made on the phone before the first send, so it survives an app restart. When the response is lost, the app shows still checking and asks the server for that same ID. The server returns the original record, so the app never sends the money twice.
card.then: Next: what the app shows when the lookup finds nothing, and how the user can retry safely.

more: The pending row also holds the amount as a Long in minor units, so 80 dollars is 8000 cents. When the response is lost, the app reads that row and queries the server with the same ID. The server answers a repeat of that ID with the original transfer's current status, not an error. So the app shows success only from the server's record.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies the pending row's fields (client transfer ID, recipient, amount in cents, pending status), explains the ID is generated on-device before the first send and survives restart, and describes the lost-response flow (show "still checking," query by the same ID, server returns the original record to prevent double-send) — consistent with the earlier client-ID sequence and server-owned ledger, with no invented employer, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W3-change1
turns.question: Your sequence ends with "save record, show result screen," which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process before the app reopens. What does the app do on relaunch with that pending row? Please update your sequence diagram.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend system and failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a known contact, with a result screen that shows success, failure, processing or unknown", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: server commits, response lost, process killed, relaunch with pending row
card.say: On relaunch, the app reads the pending row from the local database. It shows "still checking" and asks the server for that same client transfer ID. If the server has the record, the app saves the real status and shows the result. If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight. So the app never shows success or failure from a guess.
card.type: replace@A->>A: save record, show result screen: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as A's app ⏎   participant S as Wallet server ⏎   participant L as Ledger DB ⏎   A->>S: POST transfer, client ID, 8000 cents ⏎   S->>L: check A balance, debit A, credit B ⏎   L-->>S: committed ⏎   S--xA: response lost ⏎   Note over A: process killed, pending row on disk ⏎   A->>A: relaunch, read pending row ⏎   A->>S: GET transfer by client ID ⏎   S-->>A: transfer record, status success ⏎   A->>A: save record, show result screen
card.then: Next: what the app shows when the lookup finds nothing, and how the user can retry safely.

more: On relaunch the app reads the pending row and asks the server for that same client transfer ID. If the server has the record, the app saves the real status and shows the result. If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight. So the app never shows success or failure from a guess.

diagram.type: replace@A->>A: save record, show result screen: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant

judge.detail: PASS: The answer persists the client transfer ID before sending, queries the server by that same ID after relaunch, treats a missing lookup as unknown rather than failed, and relies on the server returning the original record's status for a repeat ID (no new ID, single ledger transfer).
judge.criterion: SAY and TYPE treat the outcome as unknown (not failed), persist the transfer intent ID before sending, query the server by account and that ID after restart, and replay the same intent only if the server's idempotency contract allows; the server returns the original transfer's status for a repeat of the same ID; never a new ID; ledger has one transfer.

turns.name: W3-dyn
turns.question: You said if the lookup finds nothing the state stays unknown — but what if the user, seeing "still checking," taps send again with a new client ID while the original request is still in flight?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend system and failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a known contact, with a result screen that shows success, failure, processing or unknown", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: user taps send again with a new client ID
card.say: That's the dangerous case. A new client ID looks like a new transfer, so the server could debit A twice. I'd keep the pending row and block a second send for that recipient and amount. The button would say "still checking" and only allow a retry with the same ID. Would you like me to add that guard to the design?
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer correctly identifies the double-debit risk from a new client ID, proposes blocking a second send and retrying with the same ID, and stays consistent with the earlier idempotency design without inventing new rules or background.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W4-concurrency
turns.question: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend system and failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a known contact, with a result screen that shows success, failure, processing or unknown", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: two phones, two independent 80 dollar transfers at the same time
card.say: Each phone sends its own client transfer ID, so the server treats them as two separate transfers. The server checks A's balance inside one transaction, so only one can pass. The first one commits: A goes from 100 to 20 dollars, and B goes from 0 to 80. The second one fails the balance check, because A now has only 20 dollars. That phone shows a clear failure, not unknown, and A stays at 20 dollars.
card.type: draw@: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant P1 as Phone 1 ⏎   participant P2 as Phone 2 ⏎   participant S as Wallet server ⏎   participant L as Ledger DB ⏎   P1->>S: POST transfer, client ID 1, 8000 cents ⏎   P2->>S: POST transfer, client ID 2, 8000 cents ⏎   S->>L: transaction 1: check balance, debit A, credit B ⏎   L-->>S: committed, A 20, B 80 ⏎   S-->>P1: transfer record, status success ⏎   S->>L: transaction 2: check balance, A has 20 ⏎   L-->>S: rejected, not enough balance ⏎   S-->>P2: clear failure, insufficient balance
card.then: Next: what the second phone shows, and how the user can tell it apart from the unknown state.

more: The losing phone should also refresh its balance, so it shows 20 dollars, not the old 100. And the second phone must not show "unknown" here, because the server gave a clear answer: not enough balance. So the result screen says the transfer failed, and the balance line updates to 20 dollars.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the two transfers as separate intents with distinct client IDs, checks and debits A's balance inside one transaction so only one passes, the second fails the balance check for insufficient funds, and A ends at 20 dollars.
judge.criterion: SAY treats them as two intents with separate IDs, checks and debits the balance in one transaction (row lock or conditional update), one succeeds and one fails for insufficient funds, A ends at 20 dollars.

turns.name: W5-account
turns.question: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend system and failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a known contact, with a result screen that shows success, failure, processing or unknown", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: A switches to account C, then A's old response arrives
card.say: The old response could land on C's screen and show A's money. So I'd tag every request and cache write with the account and a session generation. When the response comes back, the ViewModel checks the generation. If it's old, I drop it and don't write it to the database. A's committed transfer still lives on the server, so A sees it in history after signing in again.
card.then: Next: how the repository keeps the cache clean when two accounts share one local database.

more: The old response could land on C's screen and show A's money. So I'd tag every request and cache write with the account and a session generation. When the response comes back, the ViewModel checks the generation. If it's old, I drop it and don't write it to the database.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer tags requests and cache writes with account and session generation, drops stale responses in the ViewModel without writing to the database, prevents C from seeing A's money, and notes A's committed transfer is recovered from A's history after signing in again.
judge.criterion: SAY scopes cache writes and UI to account and session, drops callbacks from a stale session, C never sees A's data, and A's committed transfer is recovered from A's history after A signs in again.

turns.name: W6-change2
turns.question: You said the app "never shows success or failure from a guess" — now the pilot starts from a group chat saying "pay Alex for last night's dinner," with two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, and the chat stream drops right after the user confirms. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see next? And right after the user confirms, the chat stream disconnects. Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend system and failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a known contact, with a result screen that shows success, failure, processing or unknown", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting money needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has 0", "New entry flow: a group chat says pay Alex for dinner, with two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount; the chat stream drops right after the user confirms"]
card.heard: chat entry with two Alexes, no amount, stream drops after confirm
card.say: Two things change. The chat only suggests a transfer; it never authorizes one. So the app opens a native confirm screen with the amount empty, and the user picks which Alex and types the amount. If the chat stream drops after the user confirms, the payment still goes ahead, because the confirm screen already holds the details. The user sees "still checking" until the server's record comes back.
card.type: draw@new entry flow: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Chat: pay Alex for dinner] --> B[App: suggestion card] ⏎   B --> C[Native confirm screen: pick Alex, enter amount] ⏎   C --> D[Save pending row with client transfer ID] ⏎   D --> E[POST transfer to server] ⏎   E --> F[Result screen: success, failure or still checking]
card.then: Next, I'd say what the app shows if the user never picks an Alex.

more: The confirm screen is the only place that authorizes money. The server binds that approval to payer, recipient, amount and an expiry time. Chat text never authorizes a payment and never reports success. So if the stream drops, the transfer still finishes and the result screen shows the server's record.

diagram.type: draw@new entry flow: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Chat: pay Alex for dinner] --> B[App: su

judge.detail: PASS: The answer covers the key points — it asks the user to pick which Alex and type the amount, uses a native confirm screen holding the details, states the chat only suggests and never authorizes, and recovers status from the server ("still checking" until the server's record returns); the TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of the entry flow. It does not explicitly bind authorization server-side to payer/recipient/amount/expiry or tie a repeated tool call to the original intent, but it says nothing wrong and covers at least two listed points.
judge.criterion: SAY asks the user which Alex and what amount, shows a trusted native confirmation with recipient and amount, binds authorization to those parameters server-side, ties a repeated tool call to the original intent, and recovers status from the payment service when the chat drops; the model never authorizes. TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of that entry flow.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The AI trip planner at KKday is the one I'd pick.
Candidate: Travelers used it in our Android app to plan a trip they could actually book.
Candidate: They typed something like "Tokyo, 5,000 yuan, three days", and the app built a plan from real products.
Candidate: My responsibility started at the technical design and ended at launch.
Candidate: I designed the agent, built the core backend, and wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan.

Interviewer: On the AI trip planner at KKday, you said you designed the agent, built the core backend, and wrote the Android code reading the streamed plan — which of those did you personally build versus the team?
Candidate: I personally built three parts.
Candidate: First, the agent design: how it reads the request, picks real products and checks the plan.
Candidate: Second, the core backend, including the personalization data layer.
Candidate: Third, the Android code that reads the SSE stream and shows the day cards.
Candidate: The app team built the other screens, and the merchant side was not mine.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made myself is the SKU calculation on the product page.
Candidate: A user taps a date, a package or a ticket type, and the price and stock update.
Candidate: Before, every tap recalculated all combinations on the main thread and parsed the same JSON again.
Candidate: I flattened the configuration, built a price and stock index once, moved the work to Dispatchers.Default, and sent results out through StateFlow.
Candidate: Tap to finished screen went from about one second to 300 milliseconds.
Candidate: The index is built once, and a tap just looks up the result.
Candidate: The heavy work runs on Dispatchers.Default, and the UI only collects from StateFlow.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest one was a plan that looked fine but had a product that couldn't be booked.
Candidate: I first suspected the AI model, because the text read well.
Candidate: Then I replayed the saved request and response, and the model was fine.
Candidate: The real cause was our check: it compared product IDs as text, so "0123" and "123" passed as different products.
Candidate: I fixed the check to compare IDs as numbers, and added a test with that case.

Interviewer: You said replaying the saved request and response proved the model was fine — how did you confirm the "0123" vs "123" mismatch was actually the cause, rather than just a plausible theory?
Candidate: I took the same saved request and ran it through the check twice.
Candidate: First with the IDs as text, and it passed.
Candidate: Then I changed only the comparison to numbers, and it failed with the right error.
Candidate: That was the only change, so the comparison was the cause.
Candidate: I also added a test with "0123" and "123" so it can't come back.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: There were two other options.
Candidate: One was to keep the old calculation and just cache the result, but the first tap would still be slow.
Candidate: The other was to move the calculation to the backend, but that adds a network round trip on every tap.
Candidate: So I kept it on the phone with a prebuilt index.
Candidate: After release, I went through the booking flow myself and switching options felt smooth.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At Debon Securities, I was moving the trading app to new navigation.
Candidate: During testing I found some old pages had a broken back button.
Candidate: I told the project manager that same day, before I had checked every page.
Candidate: I gave two options: keep the old pages and ship the rest this week, or delay the whole release.
Candidate: He chose to keep the old pages.

Interviewer: You said the PM chose to keep the old pages and ship the rest — what risk were you willing to accept there, and who watched the data after release? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: The risk I accepted was that some old pages still had the broken back button.
Candidate: I told the PM that clearly, and he decided to ship the rest.
Candidate: I kept checking the remaining pages and fixed the back button myself.
Candidate: My change went out in the next release, after it was tested.
Candidate: For the release, we ran the main flows before shipping: open a stock, go back, and check the watchlist.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Okay, let's design the wallet.
Candidate: First, the scope I'd confirm.
Candidate: The MVP is one user path: send money to another person.
Candidate: The user picks a contact, enters an amount, confirms on a native screen, and sees the result.
Candidate: Does that match what you want?

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Okay, I'll draw the three parts and what each one owns.
Candidate: The app owns the screens and a local database.
Candidate: The local database is only a cache of what the server told us.

[board] flowchart TD |   A[App screens: send, result, history] --> B[ViewModel] |   B --> C[Repository] |   C --> D[(Local DB: cached balance and history)] |   C --> E[Wallet API client] |   E --> F[Wallet server: ledger and limits] |   F --> G[(Ledger DB)]
Candidate: The server owns the real ledger and the limits.
Candidate: The app only shows what the server told it.
Candidate: The local database is just a cache, so the UI reads from one place.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: I'll draw the sequence for A sending B 80 dollars.
Candidate: A confirms on the native screen, and the app sends the request with a client transfer ID.
Candidate: The server checks A's balance, then debits A and credits B in one transaction.
Candidate: A ends at 20 dollars and B at 80 dollars.
Candidate: The server returns the transfer record, and the app saves it and shows the result screen.

[board] sequenceDiagram |   participant A as A's app |   participant S as Wallet server |   participant L as Ledger DB |   A->>S: POST transfer, client ID, 8000 cents |   S->>L: check A balance, debit A, credit B |   L-->>S: committed |   S-->>A: transfer record, status success |   A->>A: save record, show result screen
Candidate: The sequence is on the board now.
Candidate: The next thing I'd cover is the failure path: what the app shows when the response is lost.
Interviewer: You said the app sends the request with a client transfer ID — what exactly is stored locally before that request goes out, and how does the app use that ID when the response is lost?
Candidate: Before the request goes out, I save a pending transfer row in the local database.
Candidate: It holds the client transfer ID, the recipient, the amount in cents, and a status of pending.
Candidate: The ID is made on the phone before the first send, so it survives an app restart.
Candidate: When the response is lost, the app shows still checking and asks the server for that same ID.
Candidate: The server returns the original record, so the app never sends the money twice.
Candidate: The pending row also holds the amount as a Long in minor units, so 80 dollars is 8000 cents.
Candidate: When the response is lost, the app reads that row and queries the server with the same ID.
Candidate: The server answers a repeat of that ID with the original transfer's current status, not an error.
Candidate: So the app shows success only from the server's record.

Interviewer: Your sequence ends with "save record, show result screen," which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process before the app reopens. What does the app do on relaunch with that pending row? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: On relaunch, the app reads the pending row from the local database.
Candidate: It shows "still checking" and asks the server for that same client transfer ID.
Candidate: If the server has the record, the app saves the real status and shows the result.
Candidate: If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.
Candidate: So the app never shows success or failure from a guess.

[board] save record, show result screen: sequenceDiagram |   participant A as A's app |   participant S as Wallet server |   participant L as Ledger DB |   A->>S: POST transfer, client ID, 8000 cents |   S->>L: check A balance, debit A, credit B |   L-->>S: committed |   S--xA: response lost |   Note over A: process killed, pending row on disk |   A->>A: relaunch, read pending row |   A->>S: GET transfer by client ID |   S-->>A: transfer record, status success |   A->>A: save record, show result screen
Candidate: On relaunch the app reads the pending row and asks the server for that same client transfer ID.
Candidate: If the server has the record, the app saves the real status and shows the result.
Candidate: If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.
Candidate: So the app never shows success or failure from a guess.

Interviewer: You said if the lookup finds nothing the state stays unknown — but what if the user, seeing "still checking," taps send again with a new client ID while the original request is still in flight?
Candidate: That's the dangerous case.
Candidate: A new client ID looks like a new transfer, so the server could debit A twice.
Candidate: I'd keep the pending row and block a second send for that recipient and amount.
Candidate: The button would say "still checking" and only allow a retry with the same ID.
Candidate: Would you like me to add that guard to the design?

Interviewer: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?
Candidate: Each phone sends its own client transfer ID, so the server treats them as two separate transfers.
Candidate: The server checks A's balance inside one transaction, so only one can pass.
Candidate: The first one commits: A goes from 100 to 20 dollars, and B goes from 0 to 80.
Candidate: The second one fails the balance check, because A now has only 20 dollars.
Candidate: That phone shows a clear failure, not unknown, and A stays at 20 dollars.

[board] sequenceDiagram |   participant P1 as Phone 1 |   participant P2 as Phone 2 |   participant S as Wallet server |   participant L as Ledger DB |   P1->>S: POST transfer, client ID 1, 8000 cents |   P2->>S: POST transfer, client ID 2, 8000 cents |   S->>L: transaction 1: check balance, debit A, credit B |   L-->>S: committed, A 20, B 80 |   S-->>P1: transfer record, status success |   S->>L: transaction 2: check balance, A has 20 |   L-->>S: rejected, not enough balance |   S-->>P2: clear failure, insufficient balance
Candidate: The losing phone should also refresh its balance, so it shows 20 dollars, not the old 100.
Candidate: And the second phone must not show "unknown" here, because the server gave a clear answer: not enough balance.
Candidate: So the result screen says the transfer failed, and the balance line updates to 20 dollars.
Interviewer: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?
Candidate: The old response could land on C's screen and show A's money.
Candidate: So I'd tag every request and cache write with the account and a session generation.
Candidate: When the response comes back, the ViewModel checks the generation.
Candidate: If it's old, I drop it and don't write it to the database.
Candidate: A's committed transfer still lives on the server, so A sees it in history after signing in again.
Candidate: The old response could land on C's screen and show A's money.
Candidate: So I'd tag every request and cache write with the account and a session generation.
Candidate: When the response comes back, the ViewModel checks the generation.
Candidate: If it's old, I drop it and don't write it to the database.

Interviewer: You said the app "never shows success or failure from a guess" — now the pilot starts from a group chat saying "pay Alex for last night's dinner," with two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, and the chat stream drops right after the user confirms. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see next? And right after the user confirms, the chat stream disconnects. Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.
Candidate: Two things change.
Candidate: The chat only suggests a transfer; it never authorizes one.
Candidate: So the app opens a native confirm screen with the amount empty, and the user picks which Alex and types the amount.
Candidate: If the chat stream drops after the user confirms, the payment still goes ahead, because the confirm screen already holds the details.
Candidate: The user sees "still checking" until the server's record comes back.

[board] flowchart TD |   A[Chat: pay Alex for dinner] --> B[App: suggestion card] |   B --> C[Native confirm screen: pick Alex, enter amount] |   C --> D[Save pending row with client transfer ID] |   D --> E[POST transfer to server] |   E --> F[Result screen: success, failure or still checking]
Candidate: The confirm screen is the only place that authorizes money.
Candidate: The server binds that approval to payer, recipient, amount and an expiry time.
Candidate: Chat text never authorizes a payment and never reports success.
Candidate: So if the stream drops, the transfer still finishes and the result screen shows the server's record.

Interviewer: You said the confirm screen is the only place that authorizes money — so if a group message claims transfers to Alex need no confirmation, what does the app do when the user taps that suggestion?
Candidate: The app ignores that claim.
Candidate: A message in the chat can't authorize money, so tapping the suggestion only opens the native confirm screen.
Candidate: There the user picks which Alex, types the amount, and approves.
Candidate: If the message says no confirmation is needed, the app shows a short note: payments always need your approval here.

Interviewer: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?
Candidate: Two weeks is enough for one path: send, result and history, with the pending row and the status lookup.
Candidate: Login and the ledger already exist, so I'd leave top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out.
Candidate: The tech lead and the product owner sign off, and I'd ask the founder to confirm the scope.
Candidate: For the spike, in the next half hour I'd check three things.
Candidate: First, is it a real rise in transfers, or just slow responses?

Interviewer: You said you'd check whether it's a real rise or just slow responses — so what would you personally own in that rollout, who do you need beside you, and at what point would you escalate to me?
Candidate: I'd own the Android side: the pending rows, the status lookup and what the screen shows.
Candidate: I'd need the backend owner for the ledger and the lookup, and QA to run the failure cases.
Candidate: I'd escalate to you if money could be wrong, or if we can't tell within the half hour whether a transfer went through.
Candidate: A slow screen alone I'd handle with the team.
Interviewer: That's it from me. What questions do you have for me about the team or the role?
Candidate: Yes, I have two.
Candidate: First, six months after I join, what would make you feel you hired the right Android engineer?
Candidate: Second, what's the biggest mobile challenge right now: voice response speed, partial results, or reliable actions?
